facts.claim: "My Mother Told Me (in Old Norse)" was released on 23 June 2023 by The Pagan Minstrel on the Viking Anthems EP, and it is the opening track.
The Bandcamp page credits the original song to Perly i Lotry, so this is an Old Norse cover version.
Deezer lists Perly I Lotry as the writer and composer of the track.
The Old Norse lyrics begin 'Þat mælti mín móðir / At mér skyldi kaupa / Fley ok fagrar árar'.
Bandcamp tags for the track include kravik lyre, tagelharpa, bardcore, neofolk and Old Norse. These suggest the instruments and style, but the page does not list a personnel credit.
The track was distributed via DistroKid, with the ℗ line given to The Pagan Minstrel.
The Pagan Minstrel is based in Valparaíso, Chile.
The artist's Bandcamp bio calls her a self-taught multi-instrumentalist and singer and a self-produced artist. She uses lyre, kultrun and tin whistle, among other instruments.

Other tracks on Viking Anthems are also covers: Deezer credits Valhalla Calling to Gavin Dunne, Helvegen to Einar Selvik, Trøllabundin to Eivør Pálsdóttir and Twilight of the Thunder God to Mikkonen, Söderberg and Hegg. An Old Norse version of Valhalla Calling followed as a single in January 2024.

research.lineage: The track sits in the bardcore and Nordic neofolk/pagan folk scene, drawing on Old Norse-language folk and Viking-themed music in the vein of Heilung, Einar Selvik and Eivør.

draft:
The line that does the most work in **My Mother Told Me** is the one sung twice: "Hǫggva mann ok annan." Strike down one man, then another. It lands at the end of a verse about standing tall in the prow and steering a costly ship into harbor, and the song gives it the same even weight as everything else. That flatness is the point. This is a child's boast, and in a child's boast the killing and the beautiful oars sit side by side.

The whole song is that boast, told secondhand. "Þat mælti mín móðir," it opens: my mother said. She said someone should buy me a ship and "fley ok fagrar árar," fine oars, so I could go off with the Vikings. The pride doesn't belong to the speaker alone. It is borrowed from a parent's promise, and that is why the song feels warmer than its violence suggests. Under the swagger is a kid who wants to be seen and has been told, by the person who matters most, that they will be. The lyric never squares that tenderness with the blood, and it doesn't try.

The structure makes the wish stronger than the deed. The mother's verse comes around three times and the prow-and-axe verse only twice, so the song keeps circling back to the promise and finally rests there, on leaving with the Vikings, not on the killing. Every closing line is sung twice, the way you repeat something you want to be true.

The Pagan Minstrel, a self-taught, self-produced multi-instrumentalist and singer based in Valparaíso, Chile, keeps the setting spare. Plucked strings roll out a steady arpeggio, a bowed string holds long notes underneath, and a drum keeps a driving, even pulse at a moderate walk. Her voice is clear and resonant, a single line with no harmonies, delivered strong and declarative, more storyteller than balladeer. The room sounds natural and the mix is clean, closer to a recital than to a smoky fire circle.

The song comes from Perly i Lotry, and it opens the Viking Anthems EP, a set of covers that also takes on Einar Selvik's "Helvegen" and Eivør Pálsdóttir's "Trøllabundin." That places it squarely in the bardcore and Nordic neofolk world shaped by Selvik, Eivør and Heilung, where old languages get sung over old instruments as a way of reaching back. What this version brings is restraint. It doesn't pile on drones and war chants. It trusts one voice and a few strings to carry an Old Norse lyric to listeners who mostly can't parse it, and the melody does the translating.

It sticks because you end up humming a child's promise of glory, carried by a mother's voice, before you notice what the glory was for.

factCheck.note: Matches the lyrics. The line appears twice at the end of each prow verse, and the quote is exact.

factCheck.claim: "Þat mælti mín móðir" opens the song and means 'my mother said'
factCheck.note: Matches the lyrics and the opening line cited in the researched facts.
The lyric reads "Fley ok fagrar árar". Restored the exact capitalization.

factCheck.claim: The mother's verse comes around three times and the prow-and-axe verse twice; every closing line is sung twice; the song ends on the mother's verse
factCheck.note: The lyric structure is M-P-M-P-M, and each verse ends with a doubled line.

factCheck.claim: Reading of a child's boast, borrowed pride, and unresolved tenderness and blood
factCheck.note: Interpretation resting on the lyrics. Slightly softened the assertion that the speaker is a child.
